1365.bp: When TikTok runs an experiment to test whether a new feature increases engagement, they randomly show it to some users and not others. The goal is to measure whether the feature truly caused the change in engagement, or if the difference came from random noise. But on a social network, people influence each other: if your friend sees the feature, they might tell you about it, which biases the measurement. This paper builds a system to fix that bias so TikTok's experiments give honest answers.
1365.wh: The core tension is that social networks violate a fundamental measurement assumption called SUTVA—it assumes one person's treatment doesn't spill over to affect another person's outcome. But this is obviously false on TikTok. If some users get a new feature and immediately tell their friends, the control group isn't really untreated. Earlier approaches try to cluster users into groups before the experiment to block this spillover, but static clustering is crude and misses real influence pathways. Theoretically perfect solutions exist but need computing power no production system can afford.
1365.ap: The system has three moving parts. First, instead of using a frozen social graph, they learn which users actually influence which other users by watching real interactions over time—building a dynamic interference graph that captures the true pathways influence travels. Second, they partition this massive graph into communities (groups where spillover within is tolerable but spillover between groups is blocked) using an optimized version of a clustering algorithm that Spark can run on billions of nodes daily. Third, after clustering, they measure outcomes with a variance-reduction technique called CUPED that explicitly accounts for the cluster structure, preventing the clustering itself from inflating noise.
1365.ww: Dynamic interference graphs work because influence doesn't follow a static org chart—who listens to whom depends on what they're currently talking about. By learning patterns from recent behavior, the system catches real influence, not phantom connections. The variance technique works because when you randomly assign users to clusters, you artificially introduce correlation in outcomes within each cluster; by explicitly modeling this correlation using pre-experiment data, you recover the signal buried in that noise. Together, these layers turn an impossible theoretical problem into something solvable at production scale.
1365.po: In live production, the system reduced measured interference by 68.8%, meaning far fewer treatment effects were distorted by spillover. Concretely, an experiment that looked like it gained 1.44% engagement was actually 2.08%—a significant correction that changes whether TikTok decides to ship a feature. This lets TikTok run honest experiments on a platform where influence is constant, directly improving the quality of all product decisions made from A/B tests.

1366.bp: Recommendation systems power video feeds: they pick which videos to show each person next. The goal is to show videos that person will actually watch. A good model learns from a user's history—what they've clicked, what they've watched—to guess what they'll want to see next. The payoff is clear: better recommendations mean more engagement, which is the lifeblood of a video platform.
1366.wh: Here's the catch: most people have sparse, messy watch histories. A new user has watched only a handful of videos; a casual user watches intermittently. Worse, what people watch is often driven by habit, trends, and algorithmic accidents rather than a pure signal of what they genuinely enjoy. So when you train a model purely on individual watch sequences, it learns fragile patterns from noise. And for new users, there's almost no data at all. Relying only on a person's own history also creates filter bubbles—the model just shows them more of what they already like, missing opportunities to show them something better they'd never think to search for.
1366.ap: Instead of building a model just from one user's history, the system borrows the collective wisdom: it uses a large language model to invent a semantic ID—a compact, meaningful code—for each user based on language descriptions of their interests and viewing patterns. Similarly, it creates semantic IDs for videos based on their content, titles, and metadata. Then it uses information theory to denoise both the user and video IDs, filtering out reward-driven noise (the spurious patterns that don't predict real satisfaction) while preserving signal that actually points to good matches. This multi-stage denoising happens at both the person level and the video level.
1366.ww: The intuition is that language descriptions are richer and more robust than raw click counts. An LLM can recognize that a person who watches cooking videos and DIY videos might share a common thread—they like learning and creativity—that pure behavioral data would miss. By working in this semantic space rather than raw interaction counts, the model generalizes much better to sparse data and new users. And by explicitly removing noise—the random clicks, the autopilays, the things you liked once and never again—the model learns cleaner patterns from what people truly care about. Sharing patterns across all users, not locking each person into their own bubble, means the model discovers interests people didn't know they had.
1366.po: In a production test on Alipay's video feed, the system achieved measurable gains: 0.9% lift in watch time (users watched longer), stable or improved view counts, and crucially, more diversity in what they were shown. This means the system did the hard thing—it simultaneously improved engagement and broadened what users saw, breaking the filter-bubble trap while delivering better personalization.

1367.bp: Video search ranking answers the question: when someone searches for "cooking" on TikTok, what videos should appear first? The platform has millions of short videos, and the ranking model must pick the best few thousand to show. Ranking better videos first directly translates to more users finding what they want, clicking more, and staying on the platform longer.
1367.wh: Video search at scale faces a crushing tension. Most videos get very few views—they're in the long tail. The ranking model is trained on co-occurrence: which videos do users click together, which videos do users click in sequence. This trains the model to memorize: when it sees a video that was popular, it remembers that people clicked on similar popular videos. But this strategy fails for the millions of videos with only a handful of clicks. There's no memorized pattern to fall back on. So long-tail videos get ranked low, creating a vicious cycle where they never get shown, so they accumulate even fewer clicks. Yet learning to generalize—recognizing that a video about baking is related to a video about pastry even if they were never clicked together—is equally hard without enough data.
1367.ap: The system uses two parallel ranking signals working together. One channel memorizes: it uses hashed identifiers (fingerprints) to recognize and act on exact patterns it's seen before—popular videos and their close neighbors. The other channel generalizes: it builds semantic IDs—meaning-based codes—for each video using metadata, tags, and descriptions, learned from an LLM or similar model. These semantic IDs capture that baking and pastry are related even if they weren't clicked together. The novelty is the fusion: a gating mechanism that learns, for each search and each candidate video, whether to trust the memorization channel or the generalization channel. For popular queries and videos, memorization wins. For rare, long-tail videos, generalization takes over.
1367.ww: The gating mechanism works because memorization and generalization have opposite strengths. Memorization is precise but brittle—it fails outside its training set. Generalization is flexible but risky—it can make false connections. By learning to switch between them, the model gets the best of both. On a frequent query with abundant click data, memorization has seen the patterns and is very reliable, so the gate opens to memorization. On a rare query where data is sparse, semantic similarity is more trustworthy than memorized patterns, so the gate favors generalization. Crucially, this switching is learned from data, not hand-coded, so it adapts to the distribution of every search.
1367.po: In production A/B tests, the system achieved a statistically significant 0.664% improvement in relevance metrics. More importantly, the system fixed the long-tail problem: videos that barely anyone had seen before now got shown to searchers who wanted them, because the generalization channel recognized their semantic similarity to popular queries. This grows the catalog's utility without cannibalizing popular content.

1368.bp: Platforms like TikTok care deeply about how many days users return—how many unique days per month do you open the app? Predicting whether someone will be active helps the platform decide when to send notifications, personalize content, and allocate resources. Better predictions mean better targeted engagement, which keeps people coming back.
1368.wh: The data is wildly skewed: most users are either completely inactive (they stopped using the app) or maximally active (they use it almost every day). Almost nobody uses the app on exactly 15 of 30 days; the distribution has two massive peaks at the extremes. This is the two-sided inflation problem. Traditional statistical models assume data is roughly bell-curve-shaped; they break badly on this shape. Worse, the standard approach builds a complex neural architecture to extract good features from user data, but ignores the real problem: the output distribution is severely abnormal. No amount of better features fixes a model that's predicting a bell curve when the reality is two sharp spikes.
1368.ap: Instead of building one model that tries to predict activity across all cases, the system splits the problem into two stages. First, it learns to classify: is this user at one of the extreme endpoints (fully active or completely inactive)? This is a binary decision with lots of clear signal. Second, if the user is not at an extreme, it learns to predict their activity level from the continuous distribution of the middle users. By decomposing the problem this way, the model doesn't have to fight the inflation; it acknowledges it explicitly.
1368.ww: This works because the two prediction tasks are fundamentally different. At the extremes, users are polarized: one group has very strong 'inactive' signals (hasn't opened the app in weeks), another has very strong 'active' signals (opens daily). These are easy to predict if you focus on them. For users in the middle—real, engaged users with variable behavior—the data is genuinely continuous and the modeling challenge is more nuanced. By addressing each task separately, the model avoids the impossible job of fitting one function to a bimodal shape. It's like sorting coins into dollars, quarters, and dimes before weighing them, rather than trying to build one scale that handles all three at once.
1368.po: The system was deployed on real user activity data with measurable gains in prediction accuracy and in downstream decisions like uplift modeling (deciding which users to notify to re-engage). The approach is described as simple yet effective, meaning it's practical enough to run in production and delivers real improvements without complex machinery.

1369.bp: In marketing, the big question is: if I send you an offer, will you buy more than you would have without it? Answering this question for each individual—personalized treatment decisions—is the dream of modern marketing. The payoff is enormous: companies can target offers to the people who will actually convert, saving money and improving customer satisfaction by not bombarding people with useless promotions.
1369.wh: Most real-world systems test many treatments: discount amounts (5%, 10%, 15%), communication channels (email, SMS, in-app), timing (morning, evening). When you split users into separate groups for each treatment, each group gets smaller, and data becomes sparse and imbalanced. Some treatment groups have very few users; others have many. This sparsity breaks statistical stability. Standard models struggle because they're learning from tiny, unbalanced samples. Even worse, when you have many treatments and little data per treatment, you often have access to randomized experiment data (gold standard) but it's too expensive to collect enough samples to directly learn personalized treatment effects.
1369.ap: The system uses two innovations in concert. First, a codebook layer anchors the user representation across small batches of data, stabilizing learning even when data is sparse and batch sizes fluctuate. Think of this as regularization: instead of letting the model re-invent user representations independently for each small batch, it forces the model to represent each user consistently across batches, using a learned codebook as the reference. Second, an attention layer (called Cross-Treatment Self-Attention) shares information across different treatments. If the model learns something valuable about users who get a 10% discount, it can reuse that knowledge when predicting outcomes for users who get a 15% discount. This knowledge sharing means each treatment group benefits from evidence gathered on other treatments. To extend this further, the system has a variant that learns from randomized controlled trials (experiments where the outcome is unbiased): it transfers the clean signal from RCT data into the observational data, using attention alignment and distillation.
1369.ww: Knowledge sharing across treatments works because users respond to offers along common dimensions—how price-sensitive they are, how they value the product category, how much they trust the brand. These dimensions don't change just because the discount size changed. By sharing the learned representations across treatments, the model recognizes these common factors and transfers evidence. The codebook stabilization works because it prevents the model from overfitting to the noise in small batches; instead of fitting noise, the model is forced to find consistent patterns. Using RCT data as a signal for distillation works because RCT data has no confounding—the treatment is assigned randomly, so any correlation with the outcome is causal. By using this clean causal signal to shape the predictions on observational data, the model learns to ignore spurious correlations.
1369.po: The system was deployed at Kuaishou, a major platform serving tens of millions of users. Large-scale online A/B tests showed consistent gains in personalized treatment decisions compared to baselines. This means the system can reliably identify, for each user, which offer size and channel will drive the most incremental purchase—a direct win for both the business and the user's experience.

1370.bp: Large companies like cloud providers field constant support tickets from customers: 'My database is slow,' 'I can't deploy my code,' 'The network is down.' Engineers manually write solutions, which is slow and error-prone. Imagine automating this with an AI agent—give it a ticket, and it generates a step-by-step solution. The payoff is massive: faster resolution, lower costs, less human toil. But enterprise support is unforgiving; a bad solution can cascade into real customer outages.
1370.wh: Large language models are powerful but they hallucinate: they invent confident-sounding solutions that are completely wrong or disconnected from the customer's actual situation. A generic LLM skill creator produces skills with low alignment to real support scenarios. Even worse, once a skill is deployed, there's no feedback loop. If a skill fails, nobody traces that failure back to what's wrong with the skill itself. So skills remain broken in production, accumulating failures without improving. There's a fundamental gap: skills created in the lab don't match the diversity and nuance of real tickets, and deployed skills have no way to improve.
1370.ap: The system is a closed loop. On creation, instead of using a generic prompt, a domain-aware skill creator grounds skill synthesis in the company's knowledge bases and historical support tickets. It learns from past solutions, understanding what worked in each scenario. Once a skill is deployed, a three-stage pipeline watches for failures: a Failure Analyzer examines tickets where the skill's solution didn't work, a Skill Diagnostician pinpoints what the skill misunderstood or got wrong, and a Skill Optimizer rewrites the skill to fix those deficiencies. This cycle repeats, so each generation of the skill learns from the mistakes of the previous one.
1370.ww: Grounding the initial skills in historical data works because real tickets have consistent patterns—certain issue types always appear with certain symptoms, certain solutions work for certain environments. By learning these patterns from the knowledge base, the creator avoids inventing generic nonsense. Automatic failure diagnosis works because failure is information: if the skill said to restart the database but the ticket still wasn't resolved, the diagnosis can note that restarting didn't work for this issue type and the skill should try a different approach next time. By closing this loop, the skill self-corrects over time, just like a human engineer who learns from mistakes.
1370.po: Tested on five real cloud support scenarios covering 1,883 tickets and 3,737 tasks, the system showed that domain-grounded initial skills were substantially better than generic ones. More crucially, the self-improvement loop worked: skills systematically fixed deficiencies across deployments. The result is a system that can scale support to millions of tickets while continuously improving solution quality, something a purely manual or static approach could never do.

1371.bp: E-commerce companies build recommendation systems and constantly test new ranking algorithms. The question is: which algorithm should we test in production? Testing is expensive and slow, so companies want to pre-screen candidates offline. But offline metrics like nDCG (a ranking quality score) often don't predict which algorithm users will actually prefer. So a researcher's instinct and a spreadsheet are often the final arbiter—subjective and slow. Imagine using an AI judge to evaluate which algorithm produces recommendations users prefer, quickly and cheaply, before the slow online test.
1371.wh: Manual evaluation is the current bottleneck: humans score recommendations on a scale, but humans disagree with each other, get tired, and make inconsistent judgments. Offline metrics like nDCG are math-based and reproducible but often misaligned with real user behavior. You can have algorithm A score higher on nDCG but algorithm B win online because users have preferences the math doesn't capture. So the company is stuck: slow human consensus or fast but unreliable math.
1371.ap: The system uses a large language model as a judge in two ways. First, pointwise filtering: show the LLM individual recommendations from each algorithm and ask it to rate which are good matches for the query. The LLM outputs a score, and recommendations below a quality threshold get filtered. Second, pairwise comparison: show the LLM two algorithms' recommendations for the same query side by side and ask which ranked the items better. The LLM chooses a winner. The system is designed to mitigate two common pitfalls: position bias (humans favor items shown first) by measuring consistency when you shuffle the order, and adversarial robustness (checking that the judge isn't fooled by adversarial examples).
1371.ww: LLMs work as judges because they understand semantics: they can read a product title, a query, and a recommendation, and recognize whether they match in meaning, not just in keywords. This aligns with what real users care about. For pointwise evaluation, the LLM achieves higher agreement with human consensus than human annotators achieve with each other—meaning the LLM is more stable and consistent than the flaky human baseline. For pairwise comparison, the LLM can detect subtle ranking differences: algorithm A might rank a perfect match first while algorithm B ranks a good-but-not-perfect match first; the LLM spots this and picks algorithm A. Position bias mitigation works by testing whether the judge changes its mind when you reorder recommendations; a robust judge shouldn't. Adversarial robustness checks whether the judge can be tricked by carefully constructed fake recommendations; again, robustness means the judge maintains its judgment even under adversarial pressure.
1371.po: In a large-scale online case study with over 10 million impressions, the algorithm that SAER preferred offline also achieved a statistically significant CTR lift online, providing directional evidence that LLM-based pre-screening predicts real user preference. The practical win is striking: the system produces reproducible, explainable scores in 30 minutes for 28 dollars, compared to weeks of manual labor or weeks waiting for online experiments. This dramatically accelerates the algorithm development cycle.

1372.bp: On a dating platform like Hinge, the mission is simple but hard: help people go on dates. The ranking system picks which profiles to show each user, hoping they'll swipe right, the other person will like them back, and they'll meet in person. Right now, ranking systems use swipes and matches as proxies for success. But the real win—the thing that matters—is whether that match actually leads to a conversation and a date. If the ranking system could predict what leads to actual dates, it could be much smarter.
1372.wh: Swipes and matches are noisy signals. Many matches go nowhere because one person isn't really interested in a conversation. The real bottleneck is converting matches into conversations (actual messages exchanged), not just getting a like or match. But conversations are rare and hard to predict because they depend on both people's timing, mood, and social luck, not just profile compatibility. So the system needs to model the full chain: not just 'do they like each other' but 'given that they like each other, will they actually message.'
1372.ap: The system explicitly models dating as a probabilistic chain with three links. First, the probability someone sends a like to a profile. Given they sent a like, the probability the other person matches (sends a like back). Given they matched, the probability they exchange at least one message. By breaking the outcome into this three-stage chain, the system can optimize for the final stage—conversations—rather than just the first stage. The implementation uses a multi-task learning model with two components: a shared embedding layer (shared representation of users and profiles) and a transformer architecture that reads user interaction sequences in order, capturing temporal patterns (who did you message when, how fast did they reply).
1372.ww: Modeling the chain explicitly works because each stage filters differently. At stage one, people respond to first impressions—photos, headline, vibe. At stage two, they react to the match notification and decide if they want to message. At stage three, they're both in conversation and deciding whether to keep messaging. These are three distinct decision points with different drivers. By modeling all three, the system captures the full journey instead of optimizing for an early proxy that might not correlate with dates. The transformer over sequences works because conversation patterns matter: if your last message got a response in one minute, you're likely to message again; if you waited three days and got no reply, you might be less inclined. These temporal patterns are real signals.
1372.po: In production A/B testing, the system achieved a +2.8% improvement in number of conversations and +1.4% increase in exchange coverage (how many matches actually message). These aren't flashy percentages, but on a platform where conversations directly drive revenue and mission success, they're substantial—thousands of additional real dates per month from better ranking. The ranking system went from optimizing for an intermediate goal (likes, matches) to optimizing for the actual goal (dates).

1373.bp: Imagine an AI assistant you can talk to on Amazon's website: 'I'm looking for a hiking boot that's waterproof and under 200 dollars.' The agent understands your intent, searches the catalog for matching products, asks clarifying questions, and walks you through options. The payoff is obvious: customers find products faster, answer difficult questions, and the company closes more sales. But building this at Amazon scale—millions of concurrent users—is a nightmare.
1373.wh: Research prototypes of shopping agents are slow and unreliable. They hallucinate product names and prices; they get stuck in loops asking the same question; they make up details. At production scale, serving millions of users, even small failure rates compound into massive customer frustration and revenue loss. The challenges are layered: latency (a response must come back in under a second, not thirty seconds), reliability (failures can't happen, or they'll dominate the error logs), retrieval accuracy (finding the right products matters, not just any products), tool orchestration (using the product search API, inventory system, pricing system correctly), and cost (LLM calls are expensive, and at Amazon scale, costs explode). All of this must work reliably on real traffic, not toy examples.
1373.ap: The paper doesn't detail the exact architecture but describes the approach: combine agentic reasoning (the LLM can call tools and take actions) with production-aware retrieval (finding products is optimized for real catalogs, not textbooks), tool orchestration (the system reliably calls the product search API, inventory system, and other services in the right order without hallucinating), and system optimization (latency and cost are designed in from the start, not added later). The system supports three modes: product discovery (the user asks for something and the agent suggests products), question answering (the user asks 'do these boots have good reviews?' and the agent retrieves reviews), and agentic actions (the agent can add to cart, check inventory, etc.).
1373.ww: Production-aware retrieval works because it's built for scale: instead of using a generic search, use Amazon's optimized product search which handles billion-item catalogs. Orchestration matters because LLMs hallucinate when they invent tool calls; the solution is constraining the agent to only call the tools that actually exist, with actual parameters. System optimization works by building latency and cost in from day one: use faster models where possible, cache common queries, batch requests, compress payloads. All of this means the agent is reliable because failure modes are predicted and eliminated before deployment.
1373.po: The system was deployed at Amazon scale and the paper describes the year-long journey as evidence that LLM-based agents can be reliably operated at that scale. Across millions of customers and conversations, the agent supports product discovery, question answering, and purchases without major outages. The practical result is that customers can now talk to an AI agent on Amazon, rather than manually searching and scrolling—a significant quality improvement in the shopping experience.

1374.bp: On Adobe Express, users create designs by browsing template collections—'Flyers', 'Posters', 'Social Media Templates'. These browse categories are powerful entry points: many users discover templates by exploring rather than searching. The ranking question is: within the 'Flyers' category, which templates should appear first to make users want to use them? Better-ranked templates get more clicks and usage.
1374.wh: The naive approach is to treat the collection name—'Flyers'—as a search query and use a search ranker to rank templates. But collections are curated, thematic groupings that go beyond keyword matching. The 'Flyers' collection might include templates for birthday parties, weddings, and garage sales—keyword-wise all different, but thematically aligned as 'occasions worth celebrating with a printed flyer.' A search ranker trained on query-like interactions won't capture this thematic intent. And critically, users aren't typing queries; they're browsing. They don't have a specific intent in mind, so traditional search metrics like 'did the user click on this result' are weak signals. They might click a template and scroll past, or scroll past a template and later regret it.
1374.ap: Instead of treating collections as queries, the system builds a machine-learned ranker trained directly on browse session data. A browse session is everything a user does in a category: which templates they view, which they pause on, which they click and use, and importantly, what they ignore and scroll past. This sequence of interactions is the training signal. The model learns: given that a user has browsed three templates so far without clicking, which fourth template should be shown next to maximize the chance they engage?
1374.ww: Browse sessions are richer signals than search clicks because they capture nuance. If someone clicks a template and uses it, that's a strong signal the ranking is working. If someone scrolls past a template without looking, that's a signal it shouldn't be ranked high. If someone spends time looking at a template then scrolls past, the model can learn the subtle factors that made them hesitate. Search rankers miss this; they only see the final click. A browse-session ranker sees the whole journey, so it learns what actually drives engagement in a no-query-specified scenario.
1374.po: The paper shows via offline experiments and online A/B testing that machine-learned browse ranking produces materially different rankings than treating the collection name as a query, and these differences resulted in measurable improvements to user engagement and business metrics. Users found templates that resonated with them more easily, clicked more, and converted to actual designs at higher rates. The system improved both the user experience (find better templates faster) and business outcome (more templates used).

1375.bp: Power grid operators work around the clock to prevent blackouts. When something fails—a transmission line is damaged, a substation overloads—a technician must respond. The job involves thousands of technical decisions: which breaker to open, which switch to close, which transformer to bypass. Mistakes can cascade into regional blackouts. Imagine an AI system that helps operators generate work tickets—structured instructions for technicians—that are not just plausible but physically safe and compliant with electrical constraints. The payoff is enormous: faster response, fewer dangerous mistakes, lives and infrastructure protected.
1375.wh: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a hot approach for domain-specific AI: retrieve relevant documents from a knowledge base, then use an LLM to synthesize an answer. But power grids have rigid physical laws: you cannot open a breaker and then immediately open another breaker downstream—the second breaker is now isolated and useless. These aren't suggestions; they're hard constraints. A generic RAG system might retrieve information about opening breakers and closing switches, but then generate instructions that violate the electrical topology, creating an invalid or dangerous work ticket. The fundamental problem is semantic vs. topological: the LLM understands language and semantics (a breaker is something you open), but it doesn't understand the rigid interconnection structure of the power grid (topologies).
1375.ap: The system has two pieces. First, it explicitly models the power grid topology using subgraph encoding—representing the structure of which nodes (breakers, switches, substations) are connected to which. This creates a symbolic, verifiable representation of what's physically possible. Second, it combines semantic retrieval with topological reasoning: it retrieves candidate work steps from a knowledge base, but then checks them against the topology to ensure they're valid. If a retrieved step would violate electrical constraints, it's flagged or rewritten. The paper introduces a dataset (PGWT) of real-world power grid work tickets to evaluate whether systems can reason over topology correctly.
1375.ww: This works because it separates the two kinds of reasoning. Semantic reasoning (understanding language, matching intents to actions) is what LLMs are good at. Topological reasoning (understanding physical constraints) requires explicit symbolic reasoning over the grid model. By combining both—use the LLM for semantics, use symbolic checks for topology—the system gets the best of both worlds. The symbolic topology acts as a guardrail: it catches the LLM's hallucinations before they become dangerous. Including topology-aware reasoning chains (reasoning steps that explicitly respect constraints) in the generation process means the LLM learns to generate correct solutions, not just solutions that sound plausible.
1375.po: On real-world power grid scenarios with operational noise and missing data, the system significantly outperformed state-of-the-art LLMs and generic RAG baselines. This means the system can generate work tickets that are not just semantically sensible but physically valid—tickets that a technician can execute safely without creating dangerous intermediate states. For a safety-critical domain like power grids, this is transformative: fewer mistakes, faster response, and crucially, no cascade failures from invalid instructions.

1376.bp: Music streaming platforms like Yandex Music want to quickly show users songs they'll love. When you open the app, the system runs a model that ranks millions of songs to pick the top songs to show you. The model reads your listening history and outputs a ranking. As platforms grow, users accumulate longer and longer histories (an active user might have listened to thousands of songs). Reading this history to generate a ranking becomes slow, causing delays. The goal is to rank music just as well but much faster, even as histories grow.
1376.wh: The dominant model architecture for ranking uses softmax attention—a mechanism that looks at every song in your history, computes a score for how relevant it is to the current query, and weights the history by these scores. This is powerful but has a fatal flaw: it scales quadratically with history length. A history of 100 songs requires ~10,000 operations; a history of 10,000 songs requires 100 million operations. On a fast GPU, this is still slow. But using bidirectional attention (reading the history both forwards and backwards) substantially improves quality compared to causal attention (reading only backwards). So the trade-off is clear: quadratic attention is better but slow; linear-time attention methods exist but most only support causal (one-directional) reading.
1376.ap: The system proposes Gated Bidirectional Linear Attention (GBLA), which reaches linear time (scales as history length times constant) while using bidirectional attention. It combines three lightweight tricks: local causal mixing (a small convolution that mixes nearby history items), key gating (learning to soft-forget old history), and gated normalization. These tricks are mixed into a kernelized attention mechanism (a technique for computing attention in linear time). The system doesn't replace all attention with GBLA; instead, it uses a hybrid: one traditional self-attention block followed by two GBLA blocks, repeating this pattern.
1376.ww: Linear-time attention works because you don't actually need to look at every history item equally. With kernelization (a mathematical trick), you can compute attention as a dot product of two vectors per item, rather than a full comparison of all pairs. Local causal mixing works because recent history is most relevant; you don't need to attend to songs from years ago to rank today's music. Key gating allows the model to selectively forget old items, focusing on the relevant part of the history. The hybrid approach works because not all attention needs to be linear: a small number of high-quality self-attention blocks are worth the cost, and the rest can use the fast linear layers.
1376.po: On Yandex Music's dataset with users who have histories of 32,768 songs, the system achieved an 8.2x speedup per layer compared to FlashAttention-v3 (the fastest standard implementation). Critically, the hybrid design maintained ranking quality: it produced recommendations as good as full bidirectional self-attention, but far faster. This means users see their personalized music ranking instantly instead of waiting seconds. And the approach generalized: it worked on public benchmarks outside Yandex, suggesting it's a general technique for large-scale ranking.

1377.bp: Music streaming has a massive catalog: millions of songs. When someone searches 'sad indie folk' or 'workout motivation', the system must pick the best songs, then arrange them into a playlist. The goal is to give the user a playlist they'll actually listen to, improving engagement and satisfaction. If the system is good, it turns vague emotional queries into coherent playlists that feel handpicked.
1377.wh: Most music search uses tag-based matching: songs are tagged with genres, moods, and instruments; your query is matched against these tags. This works for explicit queries like 'rock music' but breaks for implicit and subjective queries like 'songs for a road trip' or 'songs to cry to'. These queries fall outside the predefined tag vocabulary. Recently, some systems have started using LLMs to generate playlists directly: feed the LLM a query and it outputs song names. But LLMs hallucinate: they invent song names that don't exist, or suggest artists who never made the song they describe. There's a tension between tag-based (limited but reliable) and generative (flexible but unreliable).
1377.ap: The system represents each song as a structured text block combining metadata (artist, title), lyrics, and descriptive attributes. Both the user query and the song representations are encoded into a shared embedding space (a space where meaning is preserved as geometric proximity—two similar songs are nearby). This encoding is done with an LLM, so semantic meaning is captured. The system uses vector search to retrieve candidates from this embedding space, rather than exact tag matching. Then a cross-encoder (a second model) reranks the candidates by reading pairs of (query, candidate song) and scoring the match. The reranker's scores are distilled into the embedder, allowing you to serve the fast embedding search without the slow reranker at query time.
1377.ww: Embedding-based search works because it captures nuance: 'sad indie folk' isn't a tag, but if you embed it in a space where 'sad', 'indie', and 'folk' songs are nearby, the system can find songs that are close to that query. The cross-encoder reranking works because it reads the full query and candidate together, catching subtle mismatches (a song might be folk and indie but upbeat, not sad, and the reranker spots this). Distilling the reranker into the embedder works because you can use the expensive model at training time to label thousands of (query, song) pairs, then train the fast model to mimic those judgments. The result is a system that's both accurate and fast.
1377.po: In offline evaluation, the semantic vector-search pipeline achieved Precision@10 of 81% (81 out of the top 10 songs matched the query intent), substantially higher than tag-based search (64%) and better than direct LLM generation (74%). In production A/B testing on smart-speaker traffic, the system delivered double-digit relative improvements in key metrics. This means users asking for music got better playlists, better-matched to their vague emotional queries, without hallucinations or made-up songs.

1378.bp: Companies have sensitive information in their knowledge bases: contracts, private data, regulatory requirements. When an AI system retrieves and answers questions about this information, it must follow strict rules: some passages must be quoted verbatim, others must be masked entirely, others can be paraphrased. The goal is to get good answers while respecting compliance: if the system quotes a sensitive passage, that quote must be exact; if it isn't supposed to quote, the system must not accidentally quote.
1378.wh: Standard Retrieval-Augmented Generation assumes retrieved text can be freely paraphrased. The system retrieves documents and the LLM rewrites them in its own words. But in regulated domains, this is forbidden. If a contract says 'payment is due in 30 days', the system must quote exactly, not paraphrase to 'payment comes in one month'. Moreover, LLMs have a tendency to quote sensitive information even when told not to, sometimes implicitly: they might not write the exact words but reference the content in a way that reveals it. So there's a tension: allow paraphrasing and lose compliance; forbid paraphrasing and limit usefulness.
1378.ap: The system introduces a policy-guided transformation pattern. Each retrieved document segment is tagged with metadata: verbatim (must be quoted exactly), combined (can be quoted but also mixed with other evidence), or synthesis (can be paraphrased or omitted). A lightweight router looks at the query and the retrieved segment, and decides which transformation mode to use. Quote-aware templates enforce the transformation: under Verbatim mode, the LLM is forced to include the exact quote; under Synthesis, templates discourage quoting. Answer-side auditing happens after generation: the system checks the final answer to verify it adheres to policies, using response-sensitive matching (checking if sensitive content is quoted correctly) and a two-pass check to catch implicit references to sensitive content.
1378.ww: Explicit sensitivity metadata works because it captures intent: the knowledge base author marks which information is sensitive and how it should be handled, removing ambiguity. The policy-guided router works because it makes the transformation decision upfront, based on the query context, rather than leaving it to the LLM's whims. Templates work because they provide structure: under Verbatim mode, the template literally requires the LLM to fill in a direct quote, making it hard to paraphrase. Answer-side auditing works because it catches mistakes: even if the router or LLM makes a wrong choice, the audit catches unquoted sensitive content before the answer leaves the system.
1378.po: On an organizational corpus with simulated compliance constraints, the system demonstrated clear trade-offs. Under Verbatim mode, sensitive exposure risk (VVR) dropped substantially, but some models abstained from answering, reducing coverage. Under Combined (quote sensitive content, paraphrase non-sensitive), exposure risk dropped while maintaining utility. Compared to a standard RAG baseline, policy-guided Combined reduced both verbatim exposure risk and paraphrase-style sensitive reuse. The result is a system that can operate in regulated domains, balancing compliance and usefulness in a way standard RAG cannot.

1379.bp: E-commerce platforms rank products for search results. To keep rankings fresh and responsive to changing user behavior, they retrain ranking models constantly—sometimes daily. This rapid iteration means models accumulate input features (signals about products, users, queries) over months. A feature that was useful once gets left in the model; another feature becomes obsolete but lingers. The result is model bloat: the model is huge, uses memory, takes time to infer. The goal is to automatically clean up: drop features that don't help, down-weight features that have weak signals.
1379.wh: Traditional feature selection happens offline, before training starts: you run statistical tests to pick the best features, then train the model. But when data is non-stationary (the distribution of user behavior shifts monthly), offline selection is quickly outdated. Moreover, running feature selection is computationally prohibitive—testing every subset of features is exponential. And it's incompatible with streaming data: you can't batch-process a stream. So in continual learning systems, feature selection is skipped and models bloat, accumulating dead weight.
1379.ap: The system learns feature importance during training using a differentiable gate layer. Each feature has an associated gate—a learnable number between 0 and 1—that acts as a feature mask. During training, the gate is learned via backpropagation using Straight-Through Estimators (a trick for learning discrete gates via continuous relaxation). At serving time, the gates are relaxed to continuous probabilities and used as importance scores. Dead features get gates near 0 and are effectively pruned; weak features get gates below 0.5 and are down-weighted. To connect training and serving and extract interpretable scores, the system uses Probability-Scaled Average Normalization and a Two-Stage Freezing protocol (strategies to stabilize gate learning).
1379.ww: Learning gates end-to-end works because the model itself, through gradient descent, identifies which features help the loss and which don't. A feature that contributes to predicting whether a user will click gets a high gate; a feature that adds noise gets a low gate. Straight-Through Estimators work by allowing gradients to flow through the discrete gates during backpropagation, so the model can learn to turn features on or off. Two-Stage Freezing works by first training with all gates flexible, then freezing gates above/below thresholds and retraining, which stabilizes the final importance scores. The continuous relaxation at serving time works because it lets you extract a deterministic importance score (the gate value), which is interpretable and useful for monitoring.
1379.po: Deployed at Flipkart in production e-commerce search, the system pruned approximately 20% of features (dropping them entirely) and down-weighted another 25% (reducing their contribution). This reduced model size and inference latency significantly while incurring only an average AUC drop of 0.019%—essentially no loss in ranking quality. The system is scalable and interpretable: it identifies and removes dead weight automatically, and the importance scores tell engineers which features matter. This means the model stays lean and responsive even with daily retraining.
